posts.caption:
Sunday is for planning, not predicting.

Nobody knows where the market opens Monday. You don't need to. What you DO need is a plan for whatever happens.

Mark the levels on the names you trade. Check the calendar (this week has bank earnings, CPI and options expiration). Decide the most you're willing to lose this week, and write it down before the first trade.

The traders who show up prepared don't have to guess. Everyone else is reacting.

What does your Sunday prep look like? 👇
posts.comment: A plan in your head changes the moment a trade goes red. Write it down.

posts.caption:
Every trade costs money before it makes any.

Spreads, commissions and fees come out on every round trip, win or lose. They feel tiny one trade at a time. They are NOT tiny over a year.

5 trades a day at $5 per round trip = $6,300 a year.
20 trades a day at $10 per round trip = $50,400 a year.

That's before a single losing trade. Your strategy has to beat that number first just to break even.

The math: trades a day x cost per round trip x 252 trading days. Before taxes.

How many trades do you make a day? Be honest 👇

Educational only, not financial advice.
posts.comment: Spreads and fees are the one loss you're guaranteed. Your edge has to beat them first.

posts.caption:

The S&P 500 gained +1.15% this week and closed Friday at 7,811.54, less than 0.1% below the record close of 7,818.93 it set on Tuesday.

Did your portfolio beat the S&P this week? 👇

posts.caption:
Read that twice.

Most traders don't fail because their strategy is bad. They fail because they abandon it after two losses and start improvising.

Your journal is the most honest trading coach you'll ever have. It remembers exactly what happened when you followed your rules, and exactly what happened when you didn't.

Before the bell Monday: open it, read last week, and write down the ONE rule you'll protect this week.

Tag a trader who needs this before the open. 👇
posts.comment: Your journal remembers what your emotions forget. Read it before you trade.

posts.caption:
Patience isn't doing nothing. It's refusing to do the wrong thing.

Every day the market shows you dozens of moves. Most of them aren't your trade. They don't fit your setup, your size or your risk.

The traders who last aren't the ones who trade the most. They're the ones who can sit through 10 "almost" setups and only pull the trigger on the one that actually fits the plan.

Cash is a position too.

Are you a patient trader or an itchy one? 👇
posts.comment: Sitting on your hands is a skill. Most people never practice it.

posts.caption:
Calls on Friday. Puts on Saturday. Today: the COVERED CALL. Save this. 📌

You own 100 shares at $100 and sell the $105 call for $2.00. You collect $200 today, no matter what happens next.

At expiration:
→ Stock falls to $90: you lose $800 instead of $1,000 (the premium cushions it)
→ Stock stays at $100: you keep the $200
→ Stock at $105 or higher: you make $700, and that's the max. Your shares can get called away at $105

The trade-off is simple: you get paid now, you give up the big upside, and you still own the downside.

What do you want next: cash-secured puts or spreads? 👇

Hypothetical example, before commissions. Educational only, not financial advice.
posts.comment: A covered call doesn't remove the stock's downside. It only cushions it by the premium.

posts.caption:
Holding a short-dated option and "hoping" is how time decay wins. 🫠

Every day you wait, the option loses a little value. And it's not a straight line: the last few days melt the FASTEST.

That's why so many options go from "down a little" to "worth nothing" in the final week.

Simple fix: decide your exit BEFORE you enter. A profit target, a stop, and a date you'll get out by no matter what.

Ever watched one melt to zero? 👇
posts.comment: Hope is not an exit strategy. Especially with options.

posts.caption:
Would you rather... A or B? 👇

A: Catch the exact bottom once a year, but trade with no rules the rest of the time.
B: Never lose more than 1% on any trade, but never catch a bottom.

Most traders dream about A. It makes the best screenshot.

But the traders still around 10 years later usually live by B. One perfect trade can't fix a hundred careless ones, and a 1% max loss means no single trade can ever knock you out.

A or B? Tell me WHY.
posts.comment: Bottoms make great screenshots. Risk rules make careers.

posts.caption:
FOMO tells you a missed move was money taken from you. It wasn't. It was never in your account.

Here's what actually costs money: chasing the move after it already happened. Buying the top of the candle. Taking a worse entry with a bigger stop because you "can't miss this one."

A missed trade costs $0. A chased trade can cost a lot.

The market makes new setups every single day. You don't need the one that already left.

What's a trade you chased and regretted? 👇

Educational only, not financial advice.
posts.comment: The market makes a new setup every day. You don't have to take the one that already left.

posts.caption:
Funny until it's your account. 😅

This week has bank earnings on Tuesday and the CPI inflation report on Wednesday. Big event days are exactly when discipline slips: the move is fast, the screen is loud, and the plan goes out the window.

Then Thursday becomes "make it back" day. And Friday is options expiration...

Write your rules down BEFORE Monday: max loss per day, max trades per day, and what you will NOT trade.

Which day of the week is your weakest? 👇
posts.comment: If Thursday looks familiar, your max daily loss rule is missing.

WTI crude closed at $96.24 on October 6, up from $57.26 at the end of 2025.

This comes after oil hit $114.58 in April, its 2026 high.

Source: EIA via FRED. Not financial advice.
posts.comment: Oil feeds into transport, input costs and inflation. Traders watch it for a reason.

posts.caption:
Position size is the one decision you control on EVERY trade.

The 1% rule: if your stop gets hit, you lose 1% of your account. Nothing more.

The math: shares = (account x 1%) / (entry price - stop price).

$25,000 account, stop $2 below your entry: 125 shares max.
Same account, stop $5 below: 50 shares.
$10,000 account, $1 stop: 100 shares.

Notice the stop decides the size, not your confidence. A wider stop means fewer shares.

One warning: a stock can gap past your stop overnight, so the real loss can be bigger.

What % do you risk per trade? 👇

Educational only, not financial advice.
posts.comment: Size the trade off the stop, not off how confident you feel.

posts.caption:
When you watch everything, you chase everything.

Most traders have 50+ tickers on their watchlist and know almost nothing about how any of them actually move.

The best traders usually know a handful of names inside out: how they react to earnings, where buyers tend to step in, what a real breakout looks like versus a fake one.

Try this for one month: 5 tickers. That's it. Learn their personality.

How many tickers are on your list right now? 👇
posts.comment: Fewer names, better reads. Quality over quantity.

posts.caption:
Save this for Monday morning. 📌

The first hour of the trading day is decided BEFORE the bell rings.

Traders who walk in with their levels marked, the calendar checked and a max loss set don't have to improvise when the open gets wild. Everyone else is reacting.

This week especially: bank earnings Tuesday, CPI Wednesday, options expiration Friday. Know what's coming before it hits your screen.

What's the first thing you check every morning? 👇

Educational only, not financial advice.
posts.comment: Same routine every day. That's what makes it work.

posts.caption:
Margin debt just hit a record, then fell by the most ever in a single month.

FINRA data: investors borrowed a record $1.502 trillion on margin in June 2026. In July, $84.8 billion came back out, the largest one-month dollar drop since the data began in 1997.

Margin lets you buy more than you can afford. That feels amazing when the market goes up.

But it magnifies losses just as much. And if your account falls far enough, your broker can issue a margin call or sell your positions for you, at the worst possible time.

Do you trade on margin? 👇

Source: FINRA margin statistics. Not financial advice.
posts.comment: Margin calls don't wait for the market to come back.

MONDAY: Columbus Day. The stock market is OPEN, but the bond market is closed.

If you trade options through these events, remember: implied volatility tends to rise INTO big events and drop right after.

Which day are you watching most? 👇

Dates: JPMorgan investor relations, BLS, SIFMA. Not financial advice.
posts.comment: Event-heavy weeks are where position size matters most.

posts.caption:
That gap is the bid-ask spread, and you pay it every time you trade.

Buy at the $1.10 ask, and if you had to sell right away, you'd only get the $0.90 bid. That's an 18% loss before the stock even moves.

Wide spreads usually show up in options with low volume and low open interest.

How to protect yourself:
→ Check volume and open interest before you trade
→ Use limit orders, not market orders
→ Start near the middle of the spread instead of paying the ask

Do you check the spread before you buy? 👇

Educational only, not financial advice.
posts.comment: A tight spread is a free edge. A wide one is a hidden fee.

posts.caption:
More trading does not mean more money.

In a famous study of 66,465 households from 1991 to 1996, the 20% who traded the most earned 11.4% a year. The market returned 17.9%.

The researchers found it wasn't bad stock picks that hurt them. It was trading costs and trading too often.

The lesson isn't "never trade." It's that every trade needs a real reason, because every trade has a real cost.

Do you overtrade? Be honest 👇

Source: Barber & Odean, "Trading Is Hazardous to Your Wealth," Journal of Finance, 2000.
posts.comment: More trades doesn't mean more profit. Usually it means more fees.

posts.caption:
Sunday night reminder before a BIG week.

Bank earnings, CPI and options expiration all land in the next five days. It's going to be tempting to trade everything.

You don't have to. You don't have to win Monday. You don't have to make back last week. You just have to protect the account so you're still here for the setups that are actually yours.

Survive first. Profit later.

Goodnight, traders. What's your ONE rule for this week? 👇
posts.comment: Survive the week first. Profits come to the ones still standing.

posts.caption:
New week. Same rules.

Monday is when traders try to fix last week. They size up to make back a loss, chase the first move of the day, or abandon the plan they wrote on Sunday.

Don't. Last week is closed. This week has bank earnings Tuesday, the CPI report Wednesday and options expiration Friday. There will be PLENTY of chances.

Start small, follow the plan, and let the week come to you.

What's your ONE rule for this week? 👇
posts.comment: The week doesn't care how last week went. Neither should your position size.

posts.caption:
Implied volatility isn't just a number on your options chain. It's the market's estimate of how far a stock could move.

The math: expected move = price x IV x square root of (days / 365). That's a one standard deviation move, which the stock stays inside about 68% of the time.

On a $100 stock:
→ 20% IV: about ±$1.05 a day, ±$5.73 a month
→ 40% IV: about ±$2.09 a day, ±$11.47 a month
→ 80% IV: about ±$4.19 a day, ±$22.94 a month

Why it matters: if you buy an option, the stock usually has to move MORE than the market already expects for you to win. High IV means you're paying for a big move up front.

Do you check IV before you buy? 👇

Educational only, not financial advice.
posts.comment: IV is the price of uncertainty. Before earnings it's high. After earnings it usually isn't.

posts.caption:

The NYSE and Nasdaq are OPEN today. The U.S. bond market is closed, per SIFMA's holiday recommendation, so there's no cash Treasury trading.

Holiday sessions are often quieter, and quiet sessions can trap traders who force trades. The real action this week starts Tuesday with the big banks.

Are you trading today or waiting for earnings? 👇

Data: Yahoo Finance index closes, SIFMA. Not financial advice.
posts.comment: Light days are a great time to plan, not a great time to force trades.

posts.caption:
If your stop-loss could talk, this is what it would say. 👇

Moving a stop "just a little lower" feels harmless in the moment. You're not changing the plan, you're just giving it room, right?

Then you move it again. And again. And a small, planned loss becomes the trade that ruins your month.

A stop is a decision you made when you were calm. Moving it is a decision you're making when you're scared. Trust the calm version of you.

Be honest: have you ever moved a stop and regretted it? 👇
posts.comment: The stop you set before the trade is smarter than the one you'd set in the middle of it.

posts.caption:
Price tells you WHAT happened. Volume tells you how much conviction was behind it.

A stock breaking out on light volume is a few buyers pushing a thin market. Those moves often fade. A breakout on heavy volume means real money is showing up.

Same thing on the way down: a drop on huge volume is usually more serious than a slow drift lower.

Before you chase a move this morning, check one thing: is volume higher than normal? If not, be careful.

Do you watch volume or just price? 👇

Educational only, not financial advice.
posts.comment: Big candle, tiny volume? Be suspicious.

posts.caption:
Calls, puts, covered calls... today: the CASH-SECURED PUT. Save this. 📌

The stock is at $100. You sell 1 put with a $95 strike for $2.00 and collect $200 today. You set aside $9,500 in cash in case you have to buy 100 shares at $95.

At expiration:
→ Stock stays above $95: the put expires and you keep the $200
→ Stock falls below $95: you buy 100 shares at $95, but your real cost is $93 because of the premium
→ Stock drops to $85: you're down $800 on paper

It's a way to get paid while you wait to buy a stock you already want. The catch: if the stock drops hard, you still own it all the way down.

Only sell puts on stocks you'd be happy to own. Next in the series: spreads?

Hypothetical example, before commissions. Educational only, not financial advice.
posts.comment: Selling a put on a stock you don't want to own is just picking up pennies in front of a steamroller.

posts.caption:
Every blown-up account has this story somewhere in it. 😅

The first time you move a stop, nothing bad happens. The stock comes back. You feel smart.

So you do it again. And the market eventually finds the one time it doesn't come back.

Rule worth tattooing on your monitor: stops only move in ONE direction, toward locking in profit. Never further away from your entry.

Tag the friend who needs this reminder 👇
posts.comment: A stop you keep moving isn't a stop. It's a suggestion.

posts.caption:
Would you rather... A or B? 👇

A: $1,000 a month from trading, 40 hours a week at the screen.
B: $1,000 a month from dividends, zero hours a week.

Here's the catch with B: at a 4% dividend yield, $1,000 a month takes about $300,000 invested ($12,000 a year / 4%).

The catch with A: it's a job. Some months it pays more. Some months it pays nothing, or less than nothing.

One buys your time back. The other trades your time for money. A or B, and why?

Educational only, not financial advice.
posts.comment: The dream is usually trade to build the capital, then let the capital pay you.

posts.caption:
Every trader pays tuition. The question is whether you're getting an education for it.

A loss that teaches you something is part of the process. A loss you repeat three times is just a habit you haven't faced yet.

After every losing trade, write down three things: what happened, what you felt, and which rule you broke (if any). It takes two minutes.

Read it back once a week. The pattern will jump out at you.

What's a lesson the market had to teach you more than once? 👇
posts.comment: The market is an expensive teacher. Don't pay for the same class twice.

posts.caption:
We've all been the second one. 😂

Buy, panic, sell, regret, buy back higher, repeat. Every round trip costs spreads and fees, and every emotional exit locks in a loss that a plan would have avoided.

The fix isn't more screen time. It's fewer decisions: set your entry, your stop and your target BEFORE the trade, then let them do the work.

Tag the friend who trades like the second half 👇
posts.comment: If your trading looks like a ping-pong match, your plan is missing.

posts.caption:
Missing a handful of days can wipe out 20 years of returns.

$10,000 left in the S&P 500 from 2006 through 2025 grew to about $54,839 (price only, no dividends).

Miss the 10 best days and it's about $24,417.
Miss the 30 best days and you LOST money: about $9,428.

Here's the painful part: many of the best days came right after the worst ones, exactly when most people panic and sell. (More on that at 10 PM.)

Data: S&P 500 daily closes via Yahoo Finance, Dec 30, 2005 to Dec 31, 2025, price only. The best days removed, every other day kept.

Have you ever sold and watched it rip without you? 👇

Educational only, not financial advice.
posts.comment: Time in the market keeps beating timing the market.

posts.caption:
Here's a simple test for position size.

If you can't walk away from the screen for 30 minutes without your heart rate going up, the trade is too big for your account or your nerves.

The right size is boring. You know your max loss, you've accepted it before the trade, and a red candle doesn't ruin your afternoon.

Cut the size in half and watch how much better your decisions get.

Agree or disagree? 👇
posts.comment: If you can't sleep with it, you're too big.

posts.caption:
Earnings season starts TOMORROW with the big banks. Save this before you trade any of them. 📌

Earnings are the biggest scheduled risk a single stock has. The stock can gap 5%, 10% or more overnight, right past any stop you set.

And if you trade options, implied volatility usually climbs into the report and drops right after it. You can be right on direction and still lose money if the move is smaller than what was priced in.

Run through these 7 before every earnings trade.

Which earnings report are you watching this week? 👇

Educational only, not financial advice.
posts.comment: The safest earnings trade is often a smaller one.

posts.caption:
28 record closes. And we're not even through October.

The S&P 500 started 2026 with a record to beat of 6,932.05, set on Christmas Eve 2025. Since then it has closed at a new all-time high 28 times, most recently 7,818.93 on October 6.

Here's what most people get wrong: record highs FEEL like the top. Historically, they've often come in clusters during strong years, not as a single warning sign.

That doesn't mean nothing can go wrong. It means "it's too high" isn't a strategy by itself.

Are you buying records or waiting for a pullback? 👇

Data: S&P 500 daily closes via Yahoo Finance, through Oct. 9, 2026. Not financial advice.
posts.comment: Waiting for the perfect pullback has cost people more than buying at a record ever did.

If you're holding bank stocks or their options overnight, check your size tonight, not at 6:45 a.m.

Which bank are you watching? 👇

posts.comment: Big banks see the whole economy first. Their reports are a preview for everyone else.

posts.caption:
This is the part of selling options nobody explains until it happens to you.

Most stock options in the U.S. are American-style: the buyer can exercise any time before expiration. If you sold that option, you can be ASSIGNED early.

Sold a covered call? Your shares can get called away. Sold a put? You can be handed 100 shares per contract.
Early assignment is most likely when an option is deep in the money, or right before a dividend for calls.

Index options like SPX are different: they're European-style and cash-settled, so no early assignment.

Have you ever been assigned early? 👇

Educational only, not financial advice.
posts.comment: Selling options means accepting the other side's choices. Size for it.

posts.caption:
The best days and the worst days travel together.

From 2006 through 2025, 6 of the S&P 500's 10 best days came within two weeks of one of its 10 worst days.

The best day: +11.58% on October 13, 2008, just days after a -7.62% drop. In 2020, a +9.38% day on March 24 came eight days after a -11.98% crash.

That's why panic-selling is so expensive. The days you're most tempted to get out are often right next to the days you most need to be in. (That's the 4 PM table.)

Did you sell in 2020 or hold? 👇

Data: S&P 500 daily closes via Yahoo Finance, price only.
posts.comment: The recovery usually starts when it feels the worst.

posts.caption:
Earnings season starts in a few hours.

The banks report before the market opens. Futures can move overnight. And the worst place to make a trading decision is in bed at midnight with your phone 6 inches from your face.

Your plan is written. Your size is decided. Your max loss is set. Nothing you see in the next six hours changes that.

Close the app. Get some sleep. Rested traders react better.

Goodnight, traders. 🌙
posts.comment: The plan you made with a clear head beats anything you'll come up with at 2 AM.

posts.caption:
Trading desks give every trader a daily loss limit. Most people trading from home never set one.

Here's how it works. On a $10,000 account, a 2% daily limit is $200. Lose $200 and you're done. Platform closed. No exceptions.

Why it matters: three bad days in a row costs you 6%. Annoying, but fixable. One day of revenge trading can cost 20%, and a 20% loss needs a +25% gain just to get back to even.

Set yours today:
→ Pick the number BEFORE the open
→ Write it on a sticky note
→ When you hit it, walk away

Do you have a daily loss limit? What is it? 👇

Educational only, not financial advice.

#daytrading #riskmanagement #tradingpsychology #tradingrules #stockmarket
posts.comment: The best trade after hitting your limit is the one you don't take.

posts.caption:
Delta tells you more than how fast an option moves. It's also a rough probability.

Rule of thumb: an option's delta is about its chance of finishing in the money. Its chance of TOUCHING the strike before expiration is about double that.

Example: you sell a 0.20 delta put.
→ About a 20% chance it finishes in the money
→ About a 40% chance the stock trades through your strike at some point before expiration

That's why option sellers get tested far more often than they expect. Your strike getting hit is not rare. Plan for it before you sell.

These are model approximations, not guarantees. Big news can blow right through them.

Do you check delta before you pick a strike? 👇

Educational only, not financial advice.

#optionstrading #options #delta #optionsgreeks #stockmarket
posts.comment: Selling a 0.20 delta option means getting tested often. Size so a test doesn't scare you out.

posts.caption:
Not trading is a decision too. Sometimes it's the best one you'll make all day.

Forcing trades costs more than it feels like. Say you take 5 so-so trades a week that win 45% of the time at 1:1. That's -0.10R per trade on average.

Over 250 trades a year, that's -25R. Risking $100 a trade, you just paid $2,500 to feel busy.

Cash does three things for you:
→ It can't lose money while you wait
→ It keeps you ready for the A+ setup
→ It keeps your head clear

Do you trade every day or only when there's a setup? 👇

Educational only, not financial advice.

#tradingpsychology #daytrading #patience #riskmanagement #trading
posts.comment: No setup is a setup. It means wait.

posts.caption:
The easiest day to find the strongest stocks is a red day.

When the market sells off, almost everything goes down with it. The stocks that refuse to fall usually have buyers stepping in. That's relative strength.

Example from yesterday: the Nasdaq fell 0.44% while Citigroup rose 1.76%. That's 2.2 percentage points of outperformance in a single session.

How to spot it at the open:
→ Compare each stock's % change to SPY or QQQ
→ Look for green names when the index is red
→ Check that volume backs it up

Do you scan for relative strength or just for big movers? 👇

Educational only, not financial advice.

#stocktrading #relativestrength #technicalanalysis #daytrading #stockmarket
posts.comment: A stock that's green on a red day is waving at you. Put it on the list.

posts.caption:
Calls, puts, covered calls, cash-secured puts... today: the BULL CALL SPREAD. Save this. 📌

The stock is at $100. You buy the $100 call for $4.00 and sell the $110 call for $1.50. Your net cost is $250, and that's the most you can lose.

At expiration:
→ Below $100: you lose the $250
→ At $102.50: break-even
→ At $110 or higher: you make the max, $750

The trade-off: you give up everything above $110 to cut your cost from $400 to $250. A smaller bet with a clear max loss and a clear max win.

Next in the series: the bear put spread?

Hypothetical example, before commissions. Educational only, not financial advice.

Every bag holder has said this sentence at least once. 😅

It starts as a quick trade. It goes red. And instead of taking the small loss, the plan quietly changes: "I'll just hold it."

The problem is the math gets worse the longer you wait. Down 30%, you need +43% to get back. Down 50%, you need +100%.

Simple rule:
→ Decide the timeframe BEFORE you enter
→ A day trade gets a day-trade stop
→ Never turn a trade into an investment to avoid a loss

posts.caption:
Would you rather... A or B? 👇

A: a coin flip. Heads, your $10,000 account doubles to $20,000. Tails, it goes to zero.
B: +12% a year, every year, for 10 years.

Here's the math. B turns $10,000 into $31,058. A's average outcome is just $10,000, and half the time you're at zero with no way back.

That's risk of ruin. One bad outcome can end the game, and you can't compound from zero.

A or B? Be honest 👇

Educational only, not financial advice.

#wouldyourather #riskmanagement #compounding #trading #investing

posts.caption:
The most dangerous research is the kind that only proves you right.

Once you own a stock, your brain starts filtering. Good news feels important. Bad news feels like noise. That's confirmation bias, and it keeps people in losing trades far too long.

A 2-minute fix before every trade:
→ Write 3 reasons it could FAIL
→ Write the price that proves you wrong
→ Read one bearish take on purpose

If you can't explain the other side, you don't understand the trade yet.

What's a trade where you ignored the warning signs? 👇

Educational only, not financial advice.

posts.caption:
Same $1,000. Very different outcomes.

A $100 stock. Option A: buy 10 shares. Option B: buy 2 calls with a $100 strike at $5.00 each. Both cost $1,000.

At expiration:
→ Stock flat at $100: shares $0, calls -$1,000 (-100%)
→ Stock at $105: shares +$50, calls $0
→ Stock at $120: shares +$200, calls +$3,000

That's leverage, and it cuts both ways. The calls need the stock to move MORE and FASTER than the shares do, just to break even.

Hypothetical, held to expiration, before commissions.

Shares or calls, which do you usually buy? 👇

Most indicators are built from the same thing: price.

RSI, MACD, stochastics and moving averages all come from the same candles. Stack five of them and you often get the same signal five times, which feels like confirmation but isn't.

Try this:
→ Keep one for trend (like a moving average)
→ Keep one for momentum (like RSI)
→ Delete the rest for a week and just watch price and volume

A clean chart makes faster, calmer decisions.

A pump and dump is simple: promoters buy a cheap, thinly traded stock, hype it everywhere, then sell into the rush of new buyers. When they're done selling, the price collapses.

The math for the people who buy late is brutal. A $0.50 stock pumped to $1.50 that falls back to $0.50 leaves top buyers down 67%.

The SEC's Investor.gov lists these same warning signs. If a tip checks two or more boxes, walk away.

posts.caption:
This is the options mistake that costs money without anyone noticing.

Example: the stock is at $110. Your $100 call trades at $12.00 with weeks left.

→ Exercise: you buy the stock at $100 when it's worth $110. That's $1,000 of value per contract.
→ Sell the call: you collect $1,200.

The $200 difference is time value, and exercising early throws it away.

Exceptions exist, like deep in-the-money calls right before a dividend, or contracts with very wide bid-ask spreads. Most of the time, selling to close wins.

Did you know about time value when you started? 👇

Educational only, not financial advice.

posts.comment: An option is worth its intrinsic value plus time value. Exercising early keeps only the first part.

posts.caption:
The most important wall in your finances is the one between investing money and trading money.

Long-term money has one job: grow quietly for years. Trading money has a different job, and it can go to zero while you learn.

Example: put 90% of your money in long-term investments and 10% in a trading account. If the trading account goes to ZERO, you've lost 10%, not everything.

The rules:
→ Decide the split once, in writing
→ Never move long-term money to cover a trading loss
→ Add to the trading account only from new savings

Do you keep your trading money separate? 👇

posts.caption:
Cheap options feel like a bargain. The math says they're mostly lottery tickets.

Take a $100 stock and its 30-day calls (30% implied volatility, Black-Scholes):

→ $100 call: about $3.59, finishes in the money about 50% of the time
→ $110 call: about $0.66, about 13%
→ $120 call: about $0.06, about 2%

The $120 call looks cheap at six cents. But the stock has to rise more than 20% in a month just to break even, and the model gives that about a 2% chance.

Low price doesn't mean low risk. It usually means low odds.

Do you buy far out-of-the-money options? 👇

Model estimates (30 days, 30% IV, 4% rate), not guarantees. Educational only, not financial advice.

Black Monday is still the worst day in the S&P 500's history.

For perspective, the next-worst days on record:

→ Mar. 16, 2020: -11.98%

It took about a year to recover. The S&P 500 first closed back above its pre-crash level on Oct. 20, 1988.

The investors who made it back weren't the ones who guessed the bottom. They were the ones who weren't forced to sell: no margin calls, no money needed that week.

posts.caption:
The order type you pick can cost you money before the stock even moves.

Example: a stock shows $10.00 bid and $10.20 ask. A market buy fills at $10.20, or worse if the price is moving. Sell right back at the bid and you're down 2% instantly.

On 500 shares, that spread alone is $100. At the open, spreads are often wider and prices jump around.

Simple rules:
→ Use limit orders on anything that isn't super liquid
→ Be extra careful in the first minutes after the open
→ Check the bid-ask spread before you click

Market orders or limit orders, which do you use? 👇

Educational only, not financial advice.

#stocktrading #daytrading #limitorders #tradingtips #stockmarket

posts.caption:
Calls, puts, covered calls, cash-secured puts, bull call spreads... today: the BEAR PUT SPREAD. Save this. 📌

It's the bearish twin of yesterday's bull call spread. The stock is at $100. You buy the $100 put for $3.80 and sell the $90 put for $1.30. Your net cost is $250, and that's the most you can lose.

At expiration:
→ Above $100: you lose the $250
→ At $97.50: break-even
→ At $90 or lower: you make the max, $750

The trade-off: you give up gains below $90 to cut your cost from $380 to $250. You get a bearish bet with a clear max loss and a clear max win.

Next in the series: the iron condor?

Hypothetical example, before commissions. Educational only, not financial advice.

Selling too early is the most painful GOOD decision you'll ever make. 😅

If your plan said take profit at +10% and you did, you followed the plan. The stock running after doesn't make it a mistake. It makes it hindsight.

Want a middle ground? Scale out. Example: you own 100 shares at $100. Sell 50 at $110 and lock in $500. Trail a stop on the other 50 and let them run.

You'll never sell the exact top. Nobody does.

posts.caption:
Would you rather... A or B? 👇

A: win $100 nine times in a row, then lose $1,000 once.
B: lose $100 nine times in a row, then win $1,000 once.

Do the math. A ends at -100 dollars. B ends at +100 dollars.

A feels amazing 90% of the time and still loses money. B feels awful 90% of the time and still makes money. That's why win rate alone tells you almost nothing. The size of your wins and losses decides everything.

Which would you pick, honestly? 👇

Educational only, not financial advice.

#wouldyourather #tradingpsychology #riskmanagement #trading #stockmarket

posts.caption:
The price you paid is the most important number to you and the least important number to the market.

Say you bought at $50 and it's now $40. That's -20%, and getting back to $50 takes +25%. Your brain wants to wait for $50. That's anchoring.

The better question isn't "how do I get back to even?" It's "is this the best place for my money right now, at this price?"

Try this:
→ Cover your entry price on screen
→ Ask if you'd buy it today at $40
→ If the answer is no, why do you still own it?

Ever held something just to get back to even? 👇

Educational only, not financial advice.

#tradingpsychology #anchoring #behavioralfinance #investingtips #stockmarket

posts.caption:
Want to replace your salary with trading? Run these numbers first.

The return you need each year is just your income goal divided by your account size.

→ $50,000 a year from a $25,000 account: 200% a year
→ $50,000 a year from a $100,000 account: 50% a year
→ $50,000 a year from a $500,000 account: 10% a year

For perspective, the S&P 500 averaged about 8.2% a year from 1950 to 2025, price only. Needing 200% a year means needing to beat the market by roughly 25 times. Every year. Before taxes.

That's not a reason to quit. It's a reason to build the account first and the income second.

What account size would you need for your goal? 👇

Educational only, not financial advice.

#trading #personalfinance #daytrading #investing #stockmarket
posts.comment: Grow the account first. The income comes after.

posts.caption:
A good trade fits in one sentence. A bad one needs a paragraph of excuses.

Example of a real one-sentence plan: "I'm buying because it broke above $50 on double its normal volume, and I'm out if it closes back below $48."

That sentence has everything:
→ Why you're in
→ What would prove you wrong
→ Where you get out

If you can't write that sentence, you don't have a trade. You have a feeling.

Agree or disagree? 👇

posts.caption:
Save this for the next time you're tempted to "just hold it overnight." 📌

Your stop works during market hours. Overnight, a stock can open far past it, and your stop just fills at the open.

Example: a $5,000 position with a 5% stop is planned as a $250 risk. If bad news gaps it down 15% overnight, you lose $750 instead.

That's why overnight positions should be smaller than day trades.

Do you hold trades overnight? 👇

posts.caption:
Two numbers on every options chain, and most beginners mix them up.

Volume counts every contract traded today, whether it opened a new position or closed an old one. Open interest counts the contracts that are still open, and it only updates once a day, after the close.

Example: a call trades 5,000 contracts today with open interest of 1,000.
→ Tomorrow open interest jumps toward 5,000? Mostly new positions opened.
→ Open interest stays near 1,000? Mostly day trades or positions being closed.

Big volume is interesting. Big volume plus rising open interest is when new money is actually showing up.

Do you check open interest before you trade an option? 👇

Educational only, not financial advice.

#optionstrading #options #openinterest #optionseducation #stockmarket
